paragraphs.text: Capítulo 4. Nutrition

Nutrition advice is everywhere, and it's often conflicting. Eat meat. Don't eat meat. Eat breakfast. Fast until noon. Carbs are the enemy. Carbs help you burn fat. Fats are key. Fats are bad. Sugar is poison. Calories, not sugar, are what matters. Seed oils are good for you. Seed oils are bad for you... It's enough to make anyone dizzy. And there are avid debates. While some get into nuanced biochemistry, others are surprisingly basic. For example, people Still argue about whether the types of foods you eat are more important than how much you eat or whether protein guidelines are off by a factor of two. People also debate whether the timing of when you eat different types of food affects body composition—that is, your body fat to lean mass ratio. Worse, dietary fat and body fat share the same name: fat. That has millions of people avoiding certain dietary fats that, were they to eat them, would likely improve their health. I'm Old enough to remember the "low fat" trend of the early 1990s—when seemingly everything was labeled low-fat or nonfat, including things that never had fat in the first place, like soda and candy, but for which labeling as "no fat!" gave the false impression they would promote body fat los s. I also remember the 40-30-30 carbohydrateprotein-fat ratio trend, too, which was good in principle, but dificult to adhere to because—at least in my opinion—it wasn't restrictive enough to make it easy to follow. That's right, it was too permissive to allow for easy decision-making about food choices. So people ate too much. They needed to be told what not to eat. The point being: A clever way to start a diet trend is to demonize one type of food. Which may partially explain Why lowcarbohydrate and ketogenic diets became popular in the early 2010s. Eating mostly just fat and protein requires some "no thank you" discipline but is otherwise pretty simple.. untilafew weeks in, when a person realizes that even a bowl of salad is off limits and that packaged "keto" snacks often contain a lot of calories... and that calories Still matter. The rise and somewhat-fall of keto seemed to usher in time-restricted eating, or intermittent fasting, which emphasizes extended periods each day (and night) with no food intake. This approach was attractive for people who find it hard to have "just a few bites" of a certain food yet find solace knowing they can eat that same food later, once they are in their "eating window." But this diet can challenge even the most disciplined, because while it has practical, psychological, and some health benefits, it doesn't work if people eat with abandon during that window. 1 Oddly enough, a reptile from South America entered the picture and settled one major debate. Yes, a reptile. Long story, made short: The Gila monster doesn't need to eat very often. Just three to four times a year. A year! A curious biologist asked why. He discovered Gilas make a peptide called exendin-4 that potently suppresses appetite.

and their experience working with thousands of people.3 1 hosted osteopathic physician Gabrielle Lyon, DO, to discuss protein needs for both women and men, and endocrinologist Robert Lustig, MD, professor at University of California, San Francisco, about sugar.4 (P.S. Robert is not a fan of sugar!) Justin Sonnenburg, PhD, a microbiologist at Stanford and perhaps the world expert on the human gut microbiome, spoke with me about how to support a healthy gut with specific foods.5 Harvard Medical School psychiatrist Chris Palmer, MD, explained the now-demonstrated benefits of the ketogenic diet for depression and other mental health issues.6 And Satchin Panda, PhD, who directs the Regulatory Biology Laboratory at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies, in San Diego, shared his extensive knowledge on the science of intermittent fasting. These experts disagree—sometimes vehemently—on many things... no surprise there. But they also agree about many things, and one foundational understanding in particular: that when it comes to body weight, how many calories we eat relative to how many we metabolize does matter. In this chapter, you'll learn the consensus from nutrition experts that you likely have not heard anywhere else. 1'11 also share my own experience and observations, having tried many different approaches to nutrition. And I share one that is seldom discussed but that I, and many others, have used to great success. It builds on this consensus. It cuts through the noise. It puts you in the driver's seat so you can make satisfying food choices that don't sacrifice taste; that support your body composition goals; and that help ensure you get the macro- and micronutrients you need for brain and bodily health. And it can be done on a budget. The Clean Omnivore Diet I call the approach I'm suggesting here the "Clean Omnivore Diet." As you'll see in the pages that follow, this approach to nutrition is based in science. We begin, as we have for each of the topics in this book, with data. I provide an overview of nutrition to get everyone on the same page, and to help you navigate what follows. I do hope you'll read it, because I know it Will empower you, but 1'11 understand if you'd like to jump to the protocols so you can learn what to eat and when for maximal health. Body composition affects health and longevity. People with a higher ratio of lean mass to body fat tend to live longer than those with relatively higher percentages of body fat.3 More than 70 percent of Americans are overweight and more than a third are obese,2 which basically means the majority of Americans are likely shortening their lifespan with their eating habits. The harshest messaging of this I've ever heard was from an MD colleague of mine who said, "Youjust don't meet many obese eightyyear-olds." Fill in the blanks on that. Physicians are known for gallows humor, but this point matches the data. Body composition matters. The advice for most people, given the above, might simply be "lose weight." But that is short sighted. I said body composition, not weight loss. If you lose weight and much of it is muscle mass, your metabolism drops, and then it's very easy to gain the weight back. (Muscle, if you recall from chapter 2, is very metabolically active, and plays a role in blood sugar management and therefore affects insulin sensitivity, which refers to how well your body responds to increases in blood sugar.) You need to maintain and/or increase muscle mass, along with bone mass, while you lose mostly body fat. And while bone is not as sexy sounding as muscle, having adequate bone mass and density is vitally important for your health and longevity too.JO The not-so-secret secret solution? Do resistance training, and eat at what we call maintenance calories, or slightly submaintenance calories (300—500 calories less than you need per day—more on that in a moment)... unless of course you are among those trying to gain weight, in which case you want to eat a bit more (300—500) each day. In the short run, this works. But in the long run, everyone— not just those seeking to lose or gain weight— needs to eat for health and longevity, but also for taste, and in a way that is compatible with their social life, schedule, and budget. That's a tall order. The great news is that there's considerable overlap among diets that do just that—and that includes the Clean Omnivore Diet. They won't leave you avoiding restaurants, either. But they require understanding what food and nutrition are really about. WHAT TO EAT There are three macronutrients: proteins, carbohydrates, and fats. Each of these can be subdivided into categories according to how they are used by the body. Let's take a closer look at each, one at a time. How to Think About Protein Dietary proteins are foods rich in amino acids, compounds that our body needs to make its own proteins. All the cells and tissues of our body —hair, muscle, bone, et cetera—contain those proteins. So we need amino acids from food to keep our cells and tissues functional. Of the twenty amino acids found in the human body, there are nine that we cannot make on our own; they must come directly from outside sources— namely from dietary proteinn These nine amino acids are called the essential amino acids, and foods containing them are referred to as complete proteins. Many foods sourced from animals, such as red meat, poultry, fish, eggs, and shellfish, such as scallops and oysters, as well as many dairy products, contain all nine essential amino acids, and thus are considered complete proteins. Some plant-based foods such as quinoa, hemp seeds, and soy also contain all nine essential amino acids. Most plant-based foods, however, do not have all nine essential amino acids and must be combined with each other to be considered complete proteins. Examples include beans with rice, or nuts with lentils. There is a lot of debate (of course) as to whether animal-based proteins are superior to plant-based proteins, but the debate is often misleading because it neglects a key feature of any protein. And that is what I Will refer to as the complete-protein-to-calorie ratio (CP:C ratio). Even when comparing animal-based protein. They also contain some fat, or in the case of plant foods, carbohydrates and fats. Most animal-based foods like meat, eggs, and shellfish contain zero (or close to zero) carbohydrates, and varying amounts of fat. Dairy products contain protein and fat (unless defatted, like skim milk, for example), and dairy includes carbohydrates to varying degrees. So we need to ask: Does a given "protein" contain all nine essential amino acids? And: What is its CP:C ratio? In other words: How many calories of a given "protein" food do we need to eat in order to get enough of those nine essential amino acids? The answer to that question matters for body composition, health, and the pleasure you experience from eating, because getting those nine essential amino acids is crucial for satiety. That's because how much you eat at a meal is driven in part by your brain's and body's hunger for complete proteins. When you get enough complete protein, you tend to feel satisfied during, and for a long while after, the meal. When you don't, you tend to feel hungry again soon after eating. The nine amino acids are not the only reason we eat, but they are a big part of it. Below 1'11 explain how, if we don't get enough complete protein per calorie, we start to run into problems. Luckily, those problems are easy to fix. 1'11 explain how to do that too. I often hear: "But I eat protein! I eat beans, I eat peanut butter. Well, neither of those are complete proteins, but if the beans are served with rice or if the peanut butter is spread on wheat bread, then they become complete proteins. Problem solved? Usually not. In fact, often it's problem created. Remember, beans and rice together provide 6 grams of protein for every 150 calories. That means you would need to eat more than four times as many calories of beans and rice (700 calories) to hit the same amount of protein (28 grams) found in 150 calories of chicken. Peanut butter on wheat bread is a similar story, given that in those 150 calories, you're only getting 6.5 grams of protein. That brings us back to CP:C ratio. Chicken has a high ratio; beans and rice or peanut butter on wheat bread has a low ratio. To be fair, some animal-based foods also have a low CP:C ratio. Take most pork for instance. One hundred fifty calories of lean pork Will give you about the same amount of protein as 150 calories of chicken or beef (about 25 grams). But most commercially sold pork products, such as bacon, ham, and pork chops, are not lean. Most contain a high percentage of fat, and often have sugar added to them too. One hundred fifty calories of low-sugar bacon has only about 10 grams of protein. Typical store-bought bacon with sugar added? About half that, at 5 grams. You would need to eat about 400 to 500 calories of bacon to get the protein found in 150 calories of chicken. The takeaway here is that we need to prioritize eating complete protein foods, and we need to consider the CP:C ratio when selecting which to eat. While protein is not the whole story, the best nutrition plan typically places proteins with a high CP:C ratio at the center of the plate. WHAT PROTEINS ARE BEST? If you eat animal products, I suggest you prioritize lean cuts of beef, elk, venison, or bison, as well as fish and chicken. They have a high CP:C ratio. Many dairy products do, too, such as Greek and Bulgarian yogurt, and cottage cheese. Eggs are great as well, even though they do not technically meet the benchmark, given their ratio of protein to fat. That said, I Still incorporate eggs into my diet most days. After years of public debate on whether eggs are healthy or unhealthy, the FDA consensus as of 2025 is that, yes, eggs are healthy. They appear on a list right next to salmon, 100 percent olive oil, fruits, and vegetables.J2 Our grandparents were right (again!). Powdered proteins such as whey protein have a very high CP:C ratio and are a convenient way to get enough protein for perhaps a meal or snack per day, maybe two ifyou're on the go. But they should not be your only complete protein source because they lack a number of important vitamins and minerals and other micronutrients found in whole foods. You want to prioritize whole foods for that. Plant-based sources of proteins, by contrast, tend to have a low CP:C ratio. So much so that it is best not to think of most plant-based foods as proteins at all. It's more accurate to think of grains, like rice and quinoa, and legumes, like beans, simply as carbohydrates, because that's mainly what they are. And think of the lipid-rich plant-based sources of proteins, like nuts, as fats, because that's mainly what they are. There are exceptions, but by and large the CP:C ratio ofthese foods is just too low to consider them otherwise. Unless you're burning significant calories through long-duration exercise or physical labor, meal.J-3 That amount became a sort of "law" of nutrition, especially in resistance training fitness circles that prioritize muscle protein synthesis— a process that is stimulated by weight lifting, but that is also involved in muscle maintenance for everyone, lifters and non-lifters alike. Later studies showed, however, that our bodies can use pretty much any amount of protein we ingestl What changed? Mostly the conversation around protein absorption. A portion of the protein that we consume at any given meal is used by our muscles. But there's a limit to the "dose" of protein our muscles can synthesize; that dose is around 30 to 50 grams at one time.U5 Whatever amount we consume beyond that Will be absorbed by the gut and the liver, and used for things like neurotransmitter production, hair and collagen growth, immune system function, and much more. (Note that for kids Still growing, and for those who resistance train regularly, the amount directed for protein synthesis is probably closer to 40 to 50 grams per meal, with the excess available for other tasks.) Does this mean that you must consume 30 to 50 grams of protein at every meal if you want to maintain your current muscle mass? Nope. Research on intermittent fasting (a good setting to investigate this question because daily calories are consumed in a small window rather than as three meals spread across a day) found that lean muscle mass is preserved as long as enough total protein is consumed in a day.J-6 All of this explains Why people versed in nutrition don't just talk about how much protein we can absorb, but the metabolic fate of the proteins we eat. In fact, there are times when assimilating 100 grams (!) per meal is possible.J-Z Does that mean you should eat 100 grams of protein per meal? Not necessarily. First off, how many meals are you eating? And how much protein do you need? Again, we return to the data. HOW MUCH PROTEIN DO YOU NEED? Most people should aim to consume 1 gram of protein, ideally from high CP:C ratio protein sources, per pound of body weight each day. It's not crucial that you eat exactly that much every day. I suggest it as a target from which you experiment a bit to find your protein needs. If you find yourself too full or otherwise unable to hit it, that's Okay. You should never feel like you're force-feeding yourself just to hit a protein goal. Strive to hit the 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight (or close to it) most days. And if you prefer to divide your protein into multiple meals and snacks per day, do that. If, however, you prefer to eat twice a day and ingest more protein at those meals, do that, even if you're resistance training specifically to gain muscle. While it's true that spreading out your protein across four to five meals and snacks per day can provide a marginal increase in muscle protein synthesis if you're resistance training and aiming to gain the maximum amount of new muscle, the difference it makes won't be meaningful for the majority of people. So figure out the timing of your meals and snacks that works best for your hunger, energy levels, sleep, and schedule. Be mindful of, but don't obsess about, that 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight target. Some people worry that eating too much protein can cause kidney problems or gout, but the data show that only becomes an issue if people consume something in the vicinity of more than 3 grams of protein per pound of body weight—an absurdly high amount that most people would struggle to reach.U8 So don't fear eating high CP:C ratio foods. That's one more debate that's easy to settle. Another debate: There is also talk that deliberately eating far less protein than we need can help us live longer. The theory is that eating protein stimulates a rise in the level of mTOR (which stands for mammalian target of rapamycin), a protein related to cell growth that, when suppressed, has been shown to extend lifespan in animals.U2 So far, however, the data point to "NOPE" on whether a low-protein-tosuppress-mTOR diet helps humans live longer. Entire books could be devoted to any of the topics above but for now, let's just keep the CP:C ratio in the back of our minds as an important metric to consider when making food choices. Prioritizing eating enough foods with a high CP:C ratio to reach that 1 gram per pound of body weight removes a lot of confusion in the "what to eat" debate. How to Think About Carbohydrates Carbohydrates, or carbs, as we often call them, have become appropriately controversial in the last few decades. I say that because carbs include both healthy and very unhealthy varieties. And no, that's not determined by just whether a carb is complex versus simple, a term that refers to their molecular structure (more on that later). Some carbs quell hunger. Others can make you eat with abandon. Sometimes it depends what those carbs are combined with. Carbs combined with fat and with sugar, for example, can make people with a sweet tooth feel like an addict who just scored: focused on getting more. It becomes very easy to overeat. Should you just cut out all carbs? Well, cutting out carbs completely Will make you lose weight fast, but mostly you lose water weight as carbs cause you to "hold" water.2-J For most people, I don't suggest suddenly cutting out carbs completely, though cutting back on certain types of carbs can be beneficial for many people. I've seen folks with autoimmune issues resolve them by moving to a carnivore (meat, salt only) or ketogenic (very low carb) diet. Then, most gradually reintroduce carbs over time, learning which carbs are problematic for them and which are not. I have also seen people who could not lose body fat do so on very low carb diets. Ketogenic diets have also been shown to be an effective treatment for some forms of drug-resistant epilepsy22 and in some cases for schizophrenia and depression.24 Also, some people just "feel better," both mentally and physically, on a zero or near-zero carbohydrate diet. Incidentally, I am not one of those people. I love fruits and vegetables and I eat starches, but I am thoughtful about which and, to some extent, when. I also know people who have done well on an "animal-based" diet, which recommends people eat only meat, fish, eggs, and dairy. It's actually a misnomer because the actual animal-based diet made popular by Paul Saladino, MD, includes not just meat, eggs, fish, and dairy, but also fruits such as dates, bananas, cucumbers, and tomatoes (yes, those last two are fruits).25 This diet is much (after they are cooked or manufactured). Examples include rice, potatoes, beans, yams, pasta, lentils, bread, chips and crackers, and so on. When consumed with little or no added fats or sugars, non-processed starchy carbs are what some call clean starches. So if you're wondering —chips and crackers, while mostly starch, are not clean. Although fairly calorie dense, clean starches like oatmeal, potatoes, rice, beans, and lentils are terrific sources of energy because they are more slowly converted to glucose by the body. Breads made without excess sugar or preservatives such as rye bread, sourdough, and unbleached wheat bread can also be considered clean(ish) starches. That being said, you can overconsume starchy carbs.26 Four things tend to lead you there: • Ifyou don't eat enough high CP:C ratio protein along with them. • Ifyou add sugar to them including jams, honey, syrup, and more. • Ifyou add fat to them like butter, oil, or cheese. • Ifyou add both sugars and fats. Starchy carbs are easy to overconsume, in no small part because they literally melt in your mouth. They are flavorful especially when combined with fat and salt (think bread alone versus bread and butter with salt or bread dipped in olive oil with salt, or french fries, or macaroni and cheese). And when starches are combined with fat and sugar and just enough salt to bring out the sweet taste (think cheesecake, doughnuts, chocolate cake, pie, ice cream, and most breakfast cereals nowadays) most people find them super tasty, and hard to not overeat. Processed starchy carbs, like chips, crackers, storebought cookies, frozen pizza, burritos, et cetera, are basically starches with fats and/or sugar blended evenly throughout, so every bite tastes identical—identically scrumptious that is. Chips and crackers are especially easy to overconsume because they activate the "eat more of this!" circuit in your brain and body, without any of the usual satiety promoting features of whole foods. They tend to have a very low CP:C ratio, and they are incredibly calorie dense for their size. You can easily eat 800 calories of chips without feeling full... and in many cases doing that Will tend to increase your appetite. By comparison, you would have to eat about 16 ounces (a pound!) of cooked steak to get to the same 800 calories. I'm betting by the tenth ounce of steak, you're going to feel very satiated, and would stay that way for many hours. I don't want to demonize starches. I eat them. I love them. Rice and pasta dishes and a great thickcrusted rye, or sourdough bread with olive oil or butter and salt are some of my favorite foods. I also think most people can enjoy a slice of cake or pie, a scoop of ice cream, a hot dog, a slice or two of pizza, and other carb-fat-sugar combinations now and again without any issue. But even ifthey are homemade, or from a bakery or restaurant that uses quality ingredients, they should not be a Staple of anyone's diet. And the packaged, processed versions are certainly damaging to our health. This is true for a variety of reasons, but their low micronutrient value and their tendency zz to make people overeat are just two.

SO WHICH CARBS SHOULD WE EAT? Most people, unless following a ketogenic, carnivore, or animal-based diet, should consume some clean carbs one to three times per day. How much? A simple solution is to scale your starchy carb intake with the amount and type of physical activity you're doing. Unless you are Still growing, are very lean (less than 10 percent body fat for a man and less than 15 percent for a woman), or are doing a lot of cardio (1.5 hours or more per day on average) or hard manual labor (3-plus days a week), it is probably best to limit your starch intake to a third or less of your daily calories. Strive to make that from clean starches, and don't add more than one to two tablespoons of fat (butter or olive oil, etc.) to any one starch serving. And don't add sugar. If you do intense cardio or hard resistance training three or more times a week (meaning you are doing compound multi-joint exercises and take your work sets to failure; see chapter 2 for details), then consider also consuming some clean starches in the meals that follow your training session. Ideally, eat some fruit too. Long, intense cardio and resistance training of the sort described in chapter 2 can deplete your glycogen reserves" You would be wise to consume 30 to 75 grams of high CP:C ratio protein in that same meal. By the way, unless it's very intense, a yoga Class or bodyweight workout won't meaningfully deplete your glycogen reserves. Nor Will half an hour of Zone 2 running or easy laps in the swimming pool. That is not what I'm talking about. But if you push yourself running, swimming, or cycling or training with Protocol 2, you're going to want to eat starches, especially in the meal following training. There's another type of carbohydrate to discuss: fibrous carbohydrates, which as their name suggests, are high-fiber-containing carbohydrates like broccoli, cucumbers, lettuce, kale, chard, asparagus, and so on. These tend not to dissolve in your mouth, even if they are cooked first. It's hard to overstate how great complex fibrous carbs are for us. Indeed, most of us should be trying to eat more of them. They are rich with vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients and, as their name suggests, they contain a lot of fiber. We're told all the time that we need to eat more fiber, but trying to get fiber mainly from starches is a mistake. That tends to make people gain body fat, and I'm hearing from more and more people about allergy and gut issues due to eating too many grains. Look to get most of your fiber from vegetables. Though be mindful to Chew your fibrous carbs well or they can be hard on your digestive tract. And it's good to note if any specific fibrous carbs do not agree with you (you'll know!). But as a general rule, ingesting more fiber from vegetables and from low-sugar fruits is associated with better health outcomes and longevity.22 Fibrous carbs also Slow the absorption of glucose into your bloodstream for a steadier rise in your glucose levels, and they make you feel full.30 Our sense of satiety comes from a combination of having eaten enough essential amino acids and fatty acids, and from our glucose levels having risen (but not too high), but also from the mechano-sensation of the stretch sensors in our gut... which is nerd-speak for "feeling full ' There are even more benefits. As I mentioned, vegetables contain remarkably high levels of micronutrients, like vitamins, minerals, and more, and deliver those with very few calories. Whether they taste "yum," "yuck," or "meh" to you tends to be a function of age (know many kids under eight that love chard?), and how these foods are prepared. It should be obvious that adding a lot of oil or butter or sugary sauces can quickly make fibrous vegetables easy to overeat, and very calorie dense—especially if the vegetables are cooked—so add those sparingly. And we should all avoid fried vegetables, fried starches, and fried meats. Fried foods are terrible for your cardiovascular health and longevity and even have been linked to poorer mental healthn They are high in calories, often high in sodium, and can contain trans fat, which has been linked to heart disease and other bad outcomes. Ifyou're serious about your health, ditch them. If you indulge occasionally with a doughnut or French fries, no big deal. But if eating fried foods is a daily, or even a weekly habit, it Will likely catch up to you. There's one last carbohydrate relevant to this conversation. Simple carbohydrates are what are often referred to as sugars—although that can lead to a lot of confusion. Unfortunately, when most people hear the word sugar they immediately think of white table sugar, or sucrose, but simple sugars exist in many forms. Naturally occurring simple sugars in foods that have fiber and fairly high water content, like fruits or vegetables, are absorbed more slowly. The simple sugars found in honey or maple syrup, which have very little fiber, and no fat, are absorbed very quickly. Lactose, the simple sugar found in full-fat milk, is absorbed slowly because of the presence of fat. The point is that sugars vary in type, and how fast they are absorbed depends on the other macronutrients (proteins, fats, and carbs) you eat with them. Maybe you've heard that "sugar is poison." This is not true of the sugar in fruit and vegetables, or in many full-fat milk products. If your goal is to have stable blood sugar and energy levels, those sources of sugar should account for about 95 percent of your sugar intake. And while you must be careful not to overconsume maple syrup or honey and other natural liquid sweeteners—they are very dense with sugar and calories—they are not poison. So adding a small bit of pure honey or pure maple syrup to your food or drinks every so often is no big deal. Refined sugars are another story. Refined sugars are simple sugars that have been stripped of their fiber or fat content and are often chemically modified to taste extremely sweet. Some are so sweet that consuming them may change your sweet taste threshold and make otherwise savory or sweet tasting foods taste more bland.32 Luckily that effect is reversible if you cut out refined sugars even just for a few days. Sucrose, which is refined from sugarcane, is the most basic example of a refined sugar. A bit of it here or there, like table sugar in dessert, is generally not a problem for most people. Keeping refined sugars to 5 percent or less of your sugar intake is a good idea. Or, if you loathe tracking that sort of thing, simply limit yourself to one serving—a scoop of ice cream or piece of cake— per week. To some of you that may seem spartan.

Even if the packages show some amount of fiber, these foods almost always act more like sugars in the body— they get absorbed fast, and almost always lead to an overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value. While eating something fibrous (like a salad) or fatty (like almond butter) with these refined complex carbs Will typically Slow their absorption, the outcome is almost always the same: an overconsumption of calories with little nutritional value. I'm not out to demonize the packaged food industry but their goal is simple: to get you to buy and consume more of what they sell. And it's Clear they've been successful in reaching that goal given the prevalence of these foods and the declining health of those who consume them. We have plenty of evidence now linking ultra-processed foods with serious health issues, including heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, depression, and impaired sleep.36 The more cryptically problematic foods, in my opinion, are refined carbohydrates with added sugars. We don't think of them as highly processed compared to, say, chips or microwave meals, but they are nearly as bad in terms of our propensity to overeat them. Luckily there is an easier and much more satisfying way to eat. One that is affordable too. But first, we have to understand fats. How to Think About Fats First off, it's a real shame this category of macronutrients is called fats because that immediately makes people think about body fat, which almost no one wants. But you do want fats in your diet. Lipids would have been a better choice in my opinion but alas, here we are. Fats are lipids, and they are calorically dense: 9 calories per gram compared to 4 calories per gram for carbs or protein. And fats are vitally important. We can't live without them. In fact, a large part of each of our cells is made of fats, and thus consuming enough fats is crucial for cellular function and repair throughout the body. You need to eat fats, but the right kinds and the right amounts. So get it out of your mind that fats are bad. Remember, there are no essential carbohydrates, but you absolutely must eat protein and fat to survive. Fats can be broadly divided into saturated fats and unsaturated fats. The simplest way to recognize a saturated fat is that these are generally solid at room temperature. The saturated fat in cheeses and meats are good examples ofthis. While some nonanimal sources such as coconuts and Brazil nuts contain saturated fat, most saturated fats come from meat, dairy, and eggs. People love to debate if saturated fats raise your cholesterol, and it's become a circular argument because yes, they do, but then the discussion turns to if cholesterol levels, HDL and LDL (classically referred to as the good and bad cholesterols, respectively), are truly meaningful in predicting heart disease and longevity, or if there are more important metrics. The whole thing can get rather confusing.3Z Some people who eat low saturated fat diets have high LDL, due to genetics or other factors like age; some people who eat high saturated fat diets don't have high LDL, but they also tend to eat a lot of fiber, and not much starch and sugar. Pretty soon, talk turns to how insulin from carbs and not just fats impacts LDL... and the debate rages on. SO HOW MUCH FAT DO I NEED IN MY DIET? If you are eating animal-based proteins daily, and that includes eggs, red meat, or full-fat dairy, chances are good that you are getting enough saturated fat. If you are vegetarian or entirely plant-based, you might consider incorporating eggs and dairy (if vegetarian), along with coconut or coconut oil, macadamia nuts, cashews, or other foods and oils that have saturated fat. Although debated, the data show that you want only moderate amounts of saturated fats in your diet because high levels of saturated fat consumption can increase systemic inflammation—an effect that is only made worse if you also ingest sugar.3-$ Some might argue that is a consequence of eating saturated fats and carbs, not the fats per se. Yet, even if you're following a strictly ketogenic diet, excess saturated fat consumption is not good for your immediate or long-term health.32 So regardless of whether you are an omnivore, keto, or vegetarian, consuming leaner cuts of meat and emphasizing proteins with high CP:C ratios Will help keep your saturated fat intake relatively low. It's worth noting that I regularly do blood work to keep an eye on my cholesterol levels and other blood biomarkers. I think this is a good practice to truly understand how diet is affecting your blood lipids. Function Health, a company I'm an advisor to, makes this type of testing quite affordable. There are other companies entering the space as salad dressing from olive oil and using small amounts of butter here and there. No one debates olive oil's health benefits.4-W And it's delicious. As covered in chapter 2, your basal metabolism is the number of calories you burn if you were to just lie in bed all day and night and do literally nothing. This suggests that one reason people put on weight as they age is they lose muscle mass. This kind of non-exercise movement, or nonexercise activity thermogenesis (NEAT) in nerdspeak, may not seem important, but it is. While NEAT is (amazingly) a key aspect to your daily caloric expenditure, you of course can't get away with just fidgeting and walking. WHEN TO EAT Then there is the question of when we eat. Here again, people debate. In the 1990s it became popular to eat four to Six small meals per day, following a 1989 study published in the New England Journal of Medicine on the subject of "nibbling versus gorging."5Z The idea was that grazing throughout the day would prevent overeating in any one sitting and stimulate metabolism. It fell out of favor because it's impractical. It also turned out to have a trivial impact on metabolism. Most people default to eating three to four times a day, with one to two of those instances as snacks and the others as meals. Job, school, and social constraints usually dictate when, exactly, people eat. The practice of time-restricted eating, also called intermittent fasting, as discussed earlier in this chapter, became popular a few years back, and many people follow this practice either deliberately or by default because they are not hungry in the morning. They end up restricting their eating to a window of four to ten hours each 5.9 day, and most typically seven to eight hours. Some people limit themselves to one meal a day, which means their window is only one to two hours a day. There is now a fair bit of science —including clinical trials—on time-restricted eating. Intermittent fasting was made popular first as a way to lose weight and improve insulin sensitivity, meaning the extent to which our cells use glucose for energy (the more emciently this happens, the less insulin we need to produce in order to regulate blood sugar levels). Soon it was studied and touted as a tool to live longer, to avoid cancer, and on and on. When it comes to losing weight, the data show that intermittent fasting does indeed help when compared to "unrestricted eating." However, it likely helps because people end up eating fewer calories when they limit their eating to a specific time window. So ultimately, it all comes back to CICO. When you put intermittent fasting head-tohead with a diet where people can eat whenever they want, but the two diets are matched for total calories consumed, the results end up being the same. A yearlong randomized study found that people with obesity who followed a calorierestricted diet and ate only within an eighthour window did not lose more weight or body fat compared to those who followed calorie restriction without the accompanying timerestriction plan.6-W That being said, many people find it easier to control the hours in which they eat than to control the portion of what they eat, and thus find intermittent fasting a very effective tool for eating fewer calories than they would otherwise. Many people opt for intermittent fasting because they incorrectly think that means you don't have to think about the types or amount of food you eat, but if you care about your health you Still do. Fasting doesn't change our need for micronutrients. Debate continues about what it can do. Intermittent fasting has generated interest for its potential to extend life.62 However, the only strong link between fasting and extended lifespan appears to be restricting calories, not meal timing.63 That said, Satchin Panda's lab at the Salk Institute has shown that mice who eat across a twenty-four-hour window of time compared to an eight-to-twelve-hour window, even when calories are held constant, suffer negative health outcomes such as obesity, elevated glucose levels, insulin resistance, and 6.4 fatty liver. Studies from Satchin's lab have also shown similar adverse effects for humans. Further studies show that not eating within two to three hours of bedtime does seem to improve sleep quality,66 growth hormone releaseéZ sleep, and next-morning glucose regulation,6-g all of which may indirectly impact lifespan. While restricting eating within two to three hours of bedtime does seem to be a best practice, there Since I'm typically done eating around 8:00 pm., my eating window is usually eight to nine hours, maybe a bit longer. I've found that this slightly restricted window allows me to feel at my best while also helping me to manage my daily caloric intake. From a health standpoint, it's best to eat at fairly consistent times each day,Z6 but you don't have to be neurotic about it. If someone sets a dinner time for an hour earlier or later than usual, or a bit outside your eating window, it's not a huge deal. This protocol looks at the gut-brain axis, the connection between the cells in our digestive tract and specific areas of our brain. Our gut talks to our brain via two main parallel pathways. The first involves the cells in our gut communicating with our brain using a neural pathway called the vagus nerve, a bidirectional superhighway linking the organs of our body and our brain. You may remember the vagus from chapter 3. Our body and our brain are connected by a second pathway, through secreted hormones and small proteins called peptides (in general, the vagus pathway is the faster of the two). The hunger sensation arises, in part, because our stomach produces a hormone called ghrelin80 in amounts proportional to how much time has elapsed since our last meal. Ghrelin travels to our hypothalamus, a marble-sized brain region located over the roof of our mouth, where it activates our drive to seek foodu Other hormones and peptides made by both our gut and our brain make us want to eat less; for example, the peptide GLP-I gives us a feeling of fullness, which is Why GLP-I analogs are used as drugs to treat obesity. (The gut microbiome, the trillions of bacteria living in our digestive system, also influences hunger—more on that in Nutrition Protocol 6.)82 At the same time, specific nutrients in the foods we eat—most notably sugars, but also fatty acids and amino acids—activate cells in our gut called neuropod cells that communicate with the brain via the vagus nerve, leading to the release of dopamineg-3 And while dopamine does many different things in the brain and body, when it is stimulated in this context, it can drive the urge to consume more of that food. It's an elegant mechanism if you think about it, because the taste of food in our mouth is not a great indication of the actual nutrients in a given food. Taste is more of a guess, a correlate. The cells in our gut, on the other hand, are poised to respond to the broken-down components of food, letting the rest of our body and brain know what we ate and what to eat more (or less) of.
